title: Rama, freed while living
hookLine: the long talk ends, and the prince is ready to work
carry: jivanmukta: free while still living and working
tomorrow: say 'tantra' and someone smirks. what's actually in those books?

lines: THE PRINCE IS READY TO WORK.
cards: The big decision is made, and Monday still comes: emails, laundry, the last stretch of a job or a school year that suddenly feels beside the point. The Yoga Vasistha ends on a moment like that.
A long conversation is finishing. It began with a young prince who had grown thin and quiet, asking a whole court what any of it was for. Now his doubts, he says, are gone.
And what he says next is almost plain: he's ready to do his work.

teach.b: The book has a word for the person it hopes Rama will be: jivanmukta, one freed while still living. Still in a body, still with a family, still with a job to do.
It's one of Hinduism's boldest teachings: moksha, liberation, can come in this life, not only after it. They do what comes to them to do. They laugh, eat, work and grieve like anyone.
From outside, nothing marks them. Inside, nothing grips. That's where this whole run has been heading.
Rama's honest question, treated as a door. Two rams: today's effort pushing back yesterday's. Four guards at a gate, where one friend brings the rest.
Lila's room, holding a world. Chudala, free at home, and a king who had to go to the forest to learn he could come back.
Each story pointed here: not away from the world, but through it, with the grip let go. In the larger story of Rama, the forest still lies ahead of him, and a war, and a kingdom.

teach.h: NOT AWAY FROM THE WORLD, BUT THROUGH IT.
teach.b: The Yoga Vasistha doesn't take any of that away. It sends him into it free.

how: Hindu teachers in the Vedanta tradition use the word jivanmukta for one freed while living, and the Yoga Vasistha's portraits of such a person are often read aloud in their talks.

o: a guidebook of postures for a long and healthy life
a sage's long talk that sends a prince back to life free
a long poem where Rama gives up his kingdom for good

games.q: the book's ending — tap the pairs.

s: the Yoga Vasistha ends with Rama leaving the palace for the forest
he says his doubts are gone and he's ready to do his work.
jivanmukta means one freed while still living
still in a body, still with a family, still with a job to do.
in this book, a freed person stands out from everyone around them
from outside, nothing marks them; inside, nothing grips.

games.q: a coworker's big promotion starts next month, and she says this month's work doesn't count anymore. what fits the jivanmukta's way?
o: do this month's work fully, without clinging to the next.
coast; the future's settled, so today doesn't matter.
work twice as hard to prove she deserves the new job.
games.why: the jivanmukta does what comes to them to do, like anyone, with nothing gripping. the book ends with Rama ready to do his work.

practice: Bring to mind one ordinary task you've been putting off because it feels small: a reply, a thank-you, a chore. Do it now, or its first step.
When it's done, many Hindus close a task by offering it, with words like Krishnarpanam astu, may this be an offering to Krishna. Say that, or your own words of offering.
If you don't pray, simply let the task be done, without leaning on what comes of it.

wordCard.voice: The Yoga Vasistha, closing: the jivanmukta, freed while living, doing the work in front of them.

orig.note: Sanskrit jivanmukta: one freed while still living, the Yoga Vasistha's picture of the free person.

carryVoice: For the road: jivanmukta, free while still living and working. The Yoga Vasistha sends Rama back into his life free.

sources.ref: Yoga Vasistha, descriptions of the jivanmukta (one liberated while living), across the Sthiti, Upashama and Nirvana Prakaranas
Yoga Vasistha, Nirvana Prakarana, closing chapters (Rama declares his doubts dispelled)
Bhagavad Gita 9.27 (whatever you do, do it as an offering to Krishna); the common closing words Krishnarpanam astu
